messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 4 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'SSHI_FBR_Optimized': duplicate: same structure as an earlier design (c0001); nothing new was simulated. Values are tuned automatically, so propose a different structure.

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

[c0027] SSHI_FBR_Zener  (topology 40eae91a637a, score 23.27, conditions passed 1/6)
L1 L pzp n1 0.01

G1 SYNC ton=0.000158s phase=-0.235 edges=both

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$, $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$, $v_{pp} \le 0.02\text{V}$, $t_{up} \le 0.15\text{s}$, $dv \le 0.01\text{V}$.
    *   Piezo source: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p=25\text{nF}$ and $R_{leak}=20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p} \approx 3.2\text{V}$.
    *   Operating conditions: S1 (nominal), S2 (heavy load), S3 (strong excitation/light load), S4 (weak excitation), S5 (low frequency), S6 (hot/Cp+20%).
    *   Reference design (FBR) fails on ripple and startup, and fails on S2 (heavy load) and S4 (weak excitation) for $v_{avg}$.
    *   Current best (SSHI_FBR_Zener) fails on $v_{avg}$ and $t_{up}$ for most cases.

    *   Topology: L-C inverter (SSHI style) followed by a Full-Bridge Rectifier (FBR) and a Zener clamp.
    *   Issue: The output settles below 1.8V for S1, S2, S4, S5, S6.
    *   Observation: Even though the screen test shows it *can* deliver the required power (249% for S2, 951% for S4), the actual simulation results in $v_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$. This usually means the charge transfer is inefficient or the diodes are dropping too much voltage.
    *   Looking at the SSHI_FBR_Zener:
        *   `L1` (pzp, n1), `S1` (n1, pzn) creates an inductor-switch loop to flip the voltage of $C_p$.
        *   `D1-D4` form the FBR.
        *   `DZ1` is the Zener clamp.
        *   `Cout` is the storage.
    *   The problem might be that the voltage $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$ is not high enough to overcome the diode drops and the output target (1.8V) effectively after the inversion. Wait, SSHI usually increases the voltage.
    *   However, a full-bridge rectifier (FBR) has two diode drops (roughly $0.25 \times 2 = 0.5\text{V}$ for DSCH).
    *   If $V_{out} = 1.8\text{V}$, the peak piezo voltage must be at least $1.8 + 0.5 = 2.3\text{V}$ for current to flow.
    *   With $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{V}$, there is room, but the energy transfer efficiency in the current SSHI configuration might be low, or the L-S tuning is off.

    *   The previous SSHI used a bridge. A bridge is inefficient.
    *   Since we have a symmetrical source (pzp, pzn), we can use a half-bridge or a better-managed SSHI.
    *   Actually, let's look at the standard SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor).
    *   Standard SSHI usually uses a switch and an inductor to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks.
    *   Another option: SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction). SECE uses a switch to connect $C_p$ to a rectifier/storage at the peaks.
    *   SECE often performs better than SSHI in low-voltage cases because it extracts the charge more directly.

    *   Let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" or a modified SECE.
    *   In a basic SECE:
        *   The piezo is connected to a switch (S1) and a rectifier.
        *   At the peak of $V_{pzp}$, S1 closes, transferring $C_p$'s charge through a rectifier to $C_{out}$.
        *   Wait, the prompt allows SYNC switches.
    *   Let's try the "Standard SSHI" topology again but without the full bridge if possible, or a more optimized one.
    *   Actually, the most efficient simple way to extract energy from a piezo is the SECE topology:
        - Piezo terminals (pzp, pzn)
        - Switch S1 connects pzp to a rectifier (D1) which then goes to out.
        - Switch S2 connects pzn to a rectifier (D2) which then goes to out.
        - This way, we only have one diode drop per half-cycle.

    *   Wait, the prompt says: "Full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]".
    *   If I use a half-bridge:
        - S1: pzp -> n1
        - S2: pzn -> n2
        - D1: n1 -> out
        - D2: n2 -> out
        - ... but the piezo is floating. We need a return path.
    *   Let's consider the SSHI with a "diode-capacitor" (DC-DC) boost effect.
    *   Or better, a "Synchronous Rectifier" using the SYNC switches.
    *   The SYNC controller can close switches at the peaks.
    *   If we use S1 to connect pzp to out (via D1) at the positive peak, and S2 to connect pzn to out (via D2) at the negative peak... that's basically a switched-capacitor converter.

    *   Let's rethink:
        Piezo (pzp, pzn)
        S1 connects pzp to n1.
        S2 connects pzn to n1.
        D1 connects n1 to out.
        Cout at out.
        If S1 closes at the positive peak, charge flows from $C_p$ through D1 to $C_{out}$.
        If S2 closes at the negative peak, charge flows from $C_p$ (now pzn is higher than pzp) through D1 to $C_{out}$.
        This is the SECE topology. It only has one diode drop.

    *   Let's refine SECE:
        1.  S1: nodes [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1, edges: "pos", phase: 0
        2.  S2: nodes [pzn, n1], ctrl: G2, edges: "neg", phase: 0
        3.  D1: nodes [n1, out], model: "DSCH"
        4.  Cout: nodes [out, 0]
        5.  DZ1: nodes [0, out], model: "DZ33" (clamp)
        Wait, does this work? At positive peak, pzp is high, pzn is low. S1 closes, charge moves from pzp to out. At negative peak, pzn is high, pzp is low. S2 closes, charge moves from pzn to out. This effectively extracts the charge of $C_p$ twice per period.

    *   Let's check the "S4: weak excitation" case: $I_p = 30\text{uA}$. $V_{oc} = \frac{30\text{uA}}{2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 1.9\text{V}$.
    *   With one diode drop (0.25V), the available voltage is $1.9 - 0.25 = 1.65\text{V}$.
    *   Still potentially below the $1.8\text{V}$ target if the load is heavy. But S4 is light load (1000kOhm).
    *   Wait, the target is $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$. If the source voltage is only $1.9\text{V}$, a simple SECE might not reach $1.8\text{V}$ because of the diode drop.
    *   We need a boost. SSHI provides a boost by flipping the voltage.

    *   SSHI-FBR (S1-S4 bridge + L-S flip) is the standard. Why did it fail?
        - The previous SSHI_FBR_Zener had $L=10\text{mH}$ and $T_{on}=158\mu\text{s}$.
        - Let's check $T_{on} \approx \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$. For $L=10\text{mH}, C_p=25\text{nF}$, $T_{on} \approx 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} \approx 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-7}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 5 \cdot 10^{-4} \approx 1.57\text{ms}$.
        - But the SYNC `ton` is limited to $0.001\text{s}$ (1ms).
        - The tuned value was $0.000158\text{s}$ (158$\mu$s), which is much shorter than $1.57\text{ms}$. This explains the poor performance. The inversion was incomplete.

    *   Wait, if $T_{on}$ is too small, the voltage isn't flipped. If it's too large, it flips too much.
    *   Let's try a smaller $L$ to fit $T_{on}$ within the $1\text{ms}$ limit.
    *   For $T_{on} = 0.5\text{ms}$ (half the limit), $L = \frac{(T_{on}/\pi)^2}{C_p} = \frac{(0.0005/3.14)^2}{25\text{nF}} \approx \frac{2.53 \cdot 10^{-8}}{25 \cdot 10^{-9}} \approx 1\text{H}$. No, that's not right.
    *   Calculation again: $T_{on} = \pi \sqrt{LC_p} \Rightarrow L = \frac{T_{on}^2}{\pi^2 C_p}$.
    *   If $T_{on} = 1\text{ms}$, $L = \frac{10^{-6}}{9.87 \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} \approx \frac{10^{-6}}{2.47 \cdot 10^{-7}} \approx 4\text{H}$.
    *   Wait, the inductor limit is $0.01\text{H}$ (10mH).
    *   If $L = 10\text{mH}$ and $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, then $T_{on} = \pi \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = \pi \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-7}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 5 \cdot 10^{-4} \approx 1.57\text{ms}$.
    *   Since $T_{on}$ is capped at $1\text{ms}$, the maximum $T_{on}$ we can use is $1\text{ms}$.
    *   To get a full flip ($T_{on} = \pi \sqrt{LC_p}$) with $T_{on} \le 1\text{ms}$:
        $L \le \frac{(1\text{ms})^2}{\pi^2 C_p} \approx 4\text{H}$.
    *   Wait, my $T_{on}$ calculation is for a full inversion of the voltage. But $L$ is capped at $10\text{mH}$.
    *   If $L=10\text{mH}$, then $\pi \sqrt{LC_p} = 1.57\text{ms}$. The max $T_{on}$ is $1\text{ms}$.
    *   Is $1\text{ms}$ enough to flip the voltage?
    *   The voltage across $C_p$ during the switch closure follows $V(t) = V_0 \cos(\frac{t}{\sqrt{LC_p}})$.
    *   For a full flip ($V = -V_0$), we need $\frac{t}{\sqrt{LC_p}} = \pi \Rightarrow t = \pi \sqrt{LC_p}$.
    *   With $L=10\text{mH}$ and $C_p=25\text{nF}$, $t = 1.57\text{ms}$.
    *   If we can only use $T_{on} = 1\text{ms}$, the voltage becomes $V(1\text{ms}) = V_0 \cos(\frac{1\text{ms}}{\sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}}}) = V_0 \cos(\frac{0.001}{0.0005}) = V_0 \cos(2) \approx -0.416 V_0$.
    *   So we flip the voltage from $V_0$ to $-0.416 V_0$. This is still an improvement over no flip, but not a full SSHI.

    *   Wait, the reference design was a simple FBR. The SSHI_FBR_Zener should be better.
    *   Maybe the issue is the Bridge Rectifier. Two diode drops are quite a lot.
    *   What if we use a "Half-Bridge" SSHI or SECE?
    *   Let's try SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction) again, but carefully.
    *   SECE structure:
        - $S_1$ connects pzp to n1 at positive peak.
        - $S_2$ connects pzn to n1 at negative peak.
        - $D_1$ connects n1 to out.
        - $C_{out}$ is from out to 0.
        - This extracts $C_p$ voltage directly.
        - But wait, if the piezo is floating, the return path is needed.
        - Let's add $D_2$ from 0 to pzn (when $S_1$ is closed) and $D_3$ from 0 to pzp (when $S_2$ is closed).
        - This is basically a bridge where two diodes are replaced by switches.

    *   Let's try another approach: a "Charge Pump" or "Voltage Doubler" style.
    *   Since we have a SYNC, we can implement a switched-capacitor boost.
    *   Actually, the most robust high-efficiency piezo interface is the "Parallel-SSHI".
    *   But let's try a simpler "SECE-like" structure first:
        - S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1, edges: "pos", phase: 0
        - S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G2, edges: "neg", phase: 0
        - D1: [n1, out], model: "DSCH"
        - D2: [out, n2], model: "DSCH" (Wait, this is not right)

    *   Let's go back to the SSHI but use a more efficient rectifier.
    *   Instead of a bridge, can we use a "half-bridge" with a capacitor?
    *   No, the piezo is a current source.
    *   What if we use a "Zener-clamped SECE"?
        - S1: [pzp, out], ctrl: G1, edges: "pos", phase: 0
        - S2: [pzn, out], ctrl: G2, edges: "neg", phase: 0
        - This would connect pzp/pzn directly to out. But we need to prevent current from flowing back.
        - S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1, edges: "pos", phase: 0
        - D1: [n1, out], model: "DSCH"
        - S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G2, edges: "neg", phase: 0
        - (Now we need a path for the current to return to the piezo)
        - D2: [0, pzn], model: "DSCH" (at positive peak)
        - D3: [0, pzp], model: "DSCH" (at negative peak)
        - This is exactly the "bridge with two switches" I thought of.

    *   Let's try another topology: "SSHI with a capacitor instead of a bridge".
        - S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1, edges: "both"
        - L1: [n1, pzn]
        - D1: [pzp, out], model: "DSCH"
        - D2: [pzn, out], model: "DSCH"
        - D3: [0, pzp], model: "DSCH"
        - D4: [0, pzn], model: "DSCH"
        - This is just the SSHI_FBR again.

    *   Wait, there's a topology called "Symmetric SECE".
        - S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1, edges: "pos"
        - S2: [pzn, n2], ctrl: G2, edges: "neg"
        - D1: [n1, out], model: "DSCH"
        - D2: [n2, out], model: "DSCH"
        - D3: [0, n1], model: "DSCH" (Wait, no)
        - Let's try:
            S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1, edges: "pos"
            S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G2, edges: "neg"
            D1: [n1, out], model: "DSCH"
            D2: [0, pzn], model: "DSCH" (active when S1 is closed)
            D3: [0, pzp], model: "DSCH" (active when S2 is closed)
            This is basically a bridge where the two "top" diodes are replaced by switches.
            Since switches have $R_{on} = 2\Omega$, the voltage drop is much lower than a diode (0.25V).
            This should help $v_{avg}$ and $t_{up}$.

    *   Let's refine this "Switched-Bridge":
        - S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1, edges: "pos", phase: 0
        - S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G2, edges: "neg", phase: 0
        - D1: [n1, out], model: "DSCH"
        - D2: [0, pzn], model: "DSCH"
        - D3: [0, pzp], model: "DSCH"
        - DZ1: [0, out], model: "DZ33"
        - Cout: [out, 0]

    *   Let's trace the current:
        - Positive peak: pzp is high, pzn is low.
        - G1 closes S1. Current flows: pzp $\to$ S1 $\to$ n1 $\to$ D1 $\to$ out $\to$ 0 $\to$ D2 $\to$ pzn.
        - (S1 is a switch, D1 is a diode, D2 is a diode). Total drops: 2 diodes.
        - Negative peak: pzn is high, pzp is low.
        - G2 closes S2. Current flows: pzn $\to$ S2 $\to$ n1 $\to$ D1 $\to$ out $\to$ 0 $\to$ D3 $\to$ pzp.
        - Total drops: 2 diodes.
        - Wait, this is still 2 diode drops. The FBR also had 2 diode drops.
        - But in the FBR, the diodes conduct *all the time* (when $V_{piezo} > V_{out} + 2V_d$).
        - In this switched version, we only extract at the peaks. This is more like SECE.

    *   Is there a way to have only *one* diode drop?
        - If the piezo's pzn was connected to ground... but it's not.
        - If we use a capacitor to create a virtual ground?
        - Let's try the "Half-bridge" SECE:
